Dry gangrene begins at the distal part of the limb due to ischaemia. It usually occurs in the toes and feet

Wet gangrene occurs in naturally moist tissue and organs such as the mouth, bowel, lungs, cervix and vulva.

subject: Question Paper UPSC 2008
prompt: What is the treatment of breast abscess (uPsc-08)
explanation:
Note
As soon as abscess formation is complete, the treatment is inscision and drainage of pus from the abscess
cavity.
Ref: Surgery, by S. Das, page 696, fourth edition.
A l s os ee
Breast abscesses typically require treatment with surgical incision and drainage, which is usually performed
while the patient is under general anaesthesia, writes Dieter Ulitzsch, MD, from Karolinska Institute at
Danderyds Hospital in Sweden, and colleagues. ‘Recent reports have described the successful treatment of
breast abscesses with US (ultrasonography)-guided needle aspiration or catheter placement rather than with
surgical incision and drainage.’
In this study, 108 consecutive lactating women clinically suspected of breast abscess were examined with
ultrasonography, and abscesses detected by ultrasonography were treated with ultrasonographic guidance.
Of 56 abscesses revealed by ultrasonography in 43 women, 23 were smaller than 3 cm in maximum diameter
and were treated with needle aspiration, where as 33 abscesses that were 3 cm or larger were treated with
catheter insertion and drainage. except for one patient who was treated with needle aspiration and, subsequently,
underwent surgical intervention, all other women were successfully treated with ultrasonography-guided
intervention.
On a subjective pain scale of 0 to 10, mean pain score in 22 women was 2.3, suggesting that catheter placement
was well tolerated.

explanation:
Note
Lipoma is one of the commonest and most benign of all tumours.
Ref: Surgery, by S. Das, page 92, fourth edition.
A l s os ee
lipoma
Lipoma is a circumscribed mass of fat cells commonly found in the subcutaneous tissue of the arms, shoulders
and buttocks. They are also found in the peritoneal cavity in relation to the kidney, omentum or mesentery,
but very rarely in solid organs.
Ref: Illustrated, Pathology, page 131.
1326                                                                            question Paper UPSC 2008
leiomyoma
Simple tumours of muscle are derived from smooth muscle (leiomyoma), and the majority occur in the uterus
where they are extremely common. hey are firm, rounded masses which usually begin in the myometrium.
Subsequently, they may move inwards to the uterine cavity forming polypi, or outward to the serous
surface.
Occasionally, similar tumours may be found in the gastrointestinal tract, ovaries, prostate and bladder.
Degenerative changes are common in myomas. Many have a large fibrous component and, in the uterus, are
termed fibroids.
Ref: Illustrated, Pathology, page 132.
A variety of spindle cell lesions may arise in the muscle wall of any gut segment. A majority of these tumours
are of smooth muscle origin, and hence can be termed leiomyoma. The tissue of origin – smooth; nature of
tumours–benign.
Ref: Robins Pathology, seventh edition.
haematoma
Haematoma is a localized collection of blood, in a tissue. Haematomas can occur anywhere on the body.
In minor injuries, the blood is absorbed unless infection develops. Contusions (bruises) and black eyes are
familiar forms of haematoma.
Less serious types include subungual haematoma (under a finger nail or toe nail); haematoma auris (in the
tissues of the outer ear, better known as cauli ower ear).
Haematomas are associated with a fracture. They are especially serious when they occur inside the skull,
where they may place local pressure on the brain, notably epidural and subdural haematomas.
Ref: http: / / www.healthscout.com/ ency/ 68/ 677/ main.html
Fibroma
So called fibromas are extremely rare in the soft tissues. hey occur in the ovary and kidney as firm
nodules.
umours like growths of fibrous tissue also occur. Examples include:
( ) Keloid it is an overgrowth of fibrous tissue in scars. It follows radiation burns but may complicate
operation scars.
Palmar fibromatosis at first nodular, causes exion deformities of fingers (Dupuytren’s contracture) due to
contraction of fibrous tissue within the palmar fascia. A similar condition may affect the planter fascia.
Ref: Illustrated Pathology, page 130.
E xt en de di n f or m at i on
benign soft tissue tumour fundamentals:
Among the most common tumours which can be classified as benign soft tissue tumours are lipoma,
angiolipoma, fibroma, benign fibrous histiocytoma, neurofibroma, schwannoma, neurolilemmona,
haemangioma, giant cell tumour of tendon sheath and myxoma. Some conditions, like nodular fasciitis,
are not tumours, but may require similar treatment. A small number of these tumours may be related to an
underlying inherited condition.
A majority of tumours in this category are benign tumours of fat called lipomas. Lipomas frequently occur
just beneath the skin as a soft painless bulge which grows slowly over a period of months to years. These
tumours represent very little risk to the patient and can be adequately treated by a ‘marginal excision’ which is
commonly described as ‘shelling out the tumour.’ This type of treatment has a high rate of success. However,
not all of these lumps need to be removed.

Benign soft tissue tumours may or may not cause pain and vary widely in appearance.

explanation:
Note

A l s os ee
Causes of menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding)
In some cases, the cause of heavy menstrual bleeding is unknown, but a number of conditions may cause
menorrhagia. Common causes include:
(1) hormonal imbalance
In a normal menstrual cycle, a balance between the hormones oestrogen and progesterone regulates
the build up of the lining of the uterus (endometrium), which is shed during menstruation. If a
hormonal imbalance occurs, the endometrium develops in excess and eventually sheds by way
of heavy menstrual bleeding. Hormonal imbalance occurs most often in adolescent girls and in
women approaching menopause. If menorrhagia is caused by a specific hormonal imbalance, such
as thyroid disease, the heavy menstrual ow can often be controlled with hormonal medications.
However, improper use of hormonal medications can also be a direct cause of menorrhagia.
(2) Uterine fibroids
These non-cancerous (benign) tumours of the uterus appear during child-bearing years. Uterine
fibroids may cause heavier than normal or prolonged menstrual bleeding.
(3) Polyps
Small, benign growths on the lining of the uterine wall (uterine polyps) may cause heavy
or prolonged menstrual bleeding. Polyps of the uterus most commonly occur in women of
reproductive age as a result of high hormonal levels.
(4) dysfunction of the ovar ies
Lack of ovulation (anovulation) may cause hormonal imbalance and result in menorrhagia.
(5) Adenomyosis
This condition occurs when glands from the endometrium become embedded in the uterine
muscle, often causing heavy bleeding and pain. Adenomyosis is most likely to develop if you’re
a middle-aged woman who has had many children.
(6) intrauterine devi ce (iud)
Menorrhagia is a well known side effect of using a non-hormonal intrauterine device for birth control.
When an IUD is the cause of excessive menstrual bleeding, you’ll often need to remove it.
(7) Pregnancy complications
A single, heavy, late period may be due to a miscarriage. If bleeding occurs at the usual time of
menstruation, however, miscarriage is unlikely to be the cause. An ectopic pregnancy – implantation
of a fertilized egg within the fallopian tube instead of the uterus, may also cause menorrhagia.
(8)    cancer
Rarely, uterine cancer, ovarian cancer and cervical cancer can cause excessive menstrual bleeding.
(9)    Medications
Certain drugs, including antiin ammatory medications and anticoagulants (to prevent blood
clots), can contribute to heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding.
(10)   other medical conditions
A number of other medical conditions, including pelvic in ammatory disease (PID), thyroid
problems, endometriosis and liver or kidney disease, may cause menorrhagia.
Ref: http: / / www.cnn.com/ HeALTH/ library/ DS/ 00394.html

explanation:
Note

radiata.
A l s os ee
corona radiata
Corona radiata surrounds an ovum or unfertilized egg cell, and consists of two or three strata (layers) of
follicular cells. They are attached to the outer protective layer of the ovum, the zona pellucida, and their main
purpose in many animals is to supply vital proteins to the cell. They appear at ovulation, but may disappear
eventually after fertilization.
Fig: Human ovum examined fresh in the liquor folliculi. The zona pellucida is seen as a thick clear girdle
surrounded by the cells of the corona radiata.
Ref: http: / / en.wikipedia.org/ wiki/ Corona_r adiata_( embryology)
E xt en de di n f or m at i on
corpus luteum
Corpus luteum, which means ‘yellow body’ in Latin, is what is left of the follicle after a woman ovulates.
During the follicular phase of a woman’s cycle, several follicles develop under the in uence of FSH
(follicle stimulating hormone). each follicle contains an egg. In a typical cycle, only one egg will become
mature enough for ovulation. When a woman ovulates, the egg will burst from the follicle. Then what is
left of the follicle will become the corpus luteum. The luteal phase, named after the corpus luteum, is the
second half of a woman’s menstrual cycle. The luteal phase begins after ovulation and continues until
menstruation occurs.
Ref: http: / / www.justmommies.com/ articles/ corpus-luteum.shtml
1332                                                                            question Paper UPSC 2008
Primordial follicle
Within eight to ten weeks of foetal development, the primordial germ cells undergo multiple mitotic divisions
and differentiate into primordial follicles. The primordial follicle consists of a primary oocyte surrounded
by a layer of spindle-shaped granulosa cells demarcated by a basal lamina. An oocyte is considered primary
if it has not yet undergone its first meiotic division. Primordial follicles continue to multiply by mitosis and
peak at a number of approximately 7,000,000 at seven months of foetal life. Before birth, the primary oocytes
enter a final round of DNA synthesis and are then arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division until
shortly before ovulation. As such, a primary oocytes may remain in prophase I between 12 years (the onset
of puberty) and 45 years (the onset of menopause).
Ref: http: / / sprojects.mmi.mcgill.ca/ menstrualcycle/ primordialfollicle.html
Primary follicle
he granulosa cells of these primordial follicles change from a at to a cuboidal structure, marking the
beginning of the primary follicle. The oocyte genome is activated and genes become transcribed. Rudimentary
paracrine signalling pathways that are vital for communication between the follicle and oocyte are formed.
Both the oocyte and the follicle grow dramatically, increasing to almost 0.1 mm in diameter.
Primary follicles develop receptors to follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) at this time, but they are
gonadotropin-independent up until the antral stage. Research has shown, however, that the presence of FSH
accelerates follicle growth in-vitro.
A glycoprotein polymer capsule called the zona pellucida forms around the oocyte, separating it from the
surrounding granulosa cells. The zona pellucida, which remains with the oocyte after ovulation, contains
enzymes that catalyze with sperms to allow penetration.
Ref: From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia.

he most probable cause of her death is amniotic uid embolism.
A l s os ee
Amniotic fluid embolism
A rare obstetric emergency, characteri ed by entry of aminotic uid, foetal cells, hair into the mother’s
circulation through the placental bed of the uterus which triggers an allergic reaction resulting in
cardiorespiratory collapse and coagulopathy.
cause
Amniotic uid entering into maternal circulation.
Clinical features:
It has two phases:
(1) First phase: Shortness of breath. Hypotension, coma and cardiac arrest.

and excessive bleeding (due to inability to clot) and death by circulatory collapse occurs.

Amniotic uid embolism is entrance of amniotic uid and foetal cells into the maternal pulmonary circulation.
Amniotic uid embolism is a rare obstetric emergency. It usually occurs during late pregnancy, typically
during tumultuous labor and rupture of membranes but occasionally during a cesarean section. Amniotic uid
embolizes to pulmonary circulation, causing tachycardia, hypotension, respiratory failure and often rapid
death, or, in survivors, disseminated intravascular coagulation. Autopsy may show foetal squamous cells and
hair in pulmonary circulation.
Diagnosis is clinical.
Ref: The Merck Manuals Online Medical Library.
(http: / / www.merck.com/ mmpe/ sec18/ ch264/ ch264g.html)
obstructed labor
Failure to progress in labor, either because the cervix will not dilate (expand) further or (after full dilatation)
the head does not descend through the mother’s pelvis.
causes
The incidence of dystocia is enhanced by many factors including inherited large foetal size, especially in some
breeds, inherited small diameter pelvic canal, occurrence of multiple births and congenital abnormalities
which increase foetal size.
Ref: http: / / medical-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/ Obstructed+ labour
ruptured placenta (abruptio placentae)
A ruptured placenta birth injury is the detachment of placenta from the uterus before the foetus is delivered
and is also known as ‘abruptio placentae.’ A ruptured placenta birth injury is a condition in which the placenta
begins to detach and bleeding occurs. The larger the area that detaches, the greater the bleeding.
symptoms
The most common symptoms of a ruptured placenta birth injury include vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain,
nausea, thirst, fainting, blood in the amniotic uid and decreased foetal movement.
Sometimes a ruptured placenta birth injury is not diagnosed until after delivery, when clotted blood is found
behind the placenta.
treatment
There is no way of stopping placenta from rupturing during a birth injury. Treatment of the woman involved
depends on how much she is bleeding and the physical condition of her unborn baby. An immediate blood
transfusion may be required if severe blood loss has occurred.

small pox
Small pox, which is believed to have originated over 3,000 years ago in India or egypt, is one of the most

Incubation period is 12–14 days (range 7–17). During this period, the person looks and feels healthy and

he incubation period is followed by the sudden onset of in uen a-like symptoms including fever, malaise,

In latent infection, the host does not shed the infectious agent which lies dormant within the host without

Brill- inser disease
Recrudescence of epidemic typhus years after the initial attack. The agent that causes epidemic typhus
(Rickettsia prowazekii) remains viable for many years. When the host’s defenses are down, it is reactivated

After the varicella virus infects the skin, it is not completely eliminated from the body as most viruses are.
Instead, the virus travels up the nerves to important nerve branching points called ganglia, deep in the body
where they stay in an inactive or latent form. During this time the virus does not replicate. It stays in this
latent form for varying amounts of time. Certain triggers may cause the virus to travel back down the nerve
to the skin causing painful, burning blisters. This condition is known as shingles or herpes zoster (although
it is not caused by the herpes virus) or varicella zoster or just zoster. Shingles occurs in about 20 per cent of

The effects of hookworm will depend upon the duration and severity of the infection. The abdominal pain,

heart symptoms should gradually improve as well.
herpes simplex
An infection by herpes simplex virus is marked by watery blisters in the skin or mucous membrane of the
mouth, lips or genitals. Lesions heal with a scab characteristic of herpetic disease. However, the infection is
persistent and symptoms may recur periodically as outbreaks of sores near the site of original infection. After
the initial or primary infection, herpes simplex virus becomes latent in the cell bodies of nerves in the area.

virus via the nerve’s axon to the skin, where virus replication and shedding occurs.

dynamic action

Common to all the members of certain class of drugs which serve to distinguish this class from others but

concordance repertory
Concordance (Puritan) group insists on maintaining the purity of symptoms as described and recorded in
the words of the provers or physicians. Puritan groups of repertories are good for reference purpose where
the clear cut symptoms with their peculiarities are present. But it is not at all good for repertorization by
artithmatic calculation of the totality. This group is called Concordance Repertories.
Examples:
Dr C.B. Knerr’s Repertory of Hering’s Guiding Symptoms of Our Materia Medica.
Dr W. D. Gentry’s Concordance Repertory.
Ref: Reperire, by Dr Vidyadhar R. Khanaj, page 70, 71.
First card repertory
In       , William afferson Guernsey, prepared the first card repertory based on Boenninghausen’s works
that is, Guernsey’s Boenninghausen’s slips published by Globe Press, Philadelphia. Before that in 1885,
he prepared a Card Repertory for Diphtheria, which was printed in Homoeopathic Physician in 25 pages.
Guernsey’s Bonninghausen’s slips had 2467 cards plus a book of 57 pages, a box 16.5” x 19.5” x 6.50”
compartments each containing 49 slips, 13.5” x1.5” wide. each slop of paper represented a single rubric, and
had printed upon it in a column the grades of the remedies in alphabetical order. he first slip contained a
columnar list of all the remedies. When the slips were all lined up next to the first slop, the grading , 2, ,
would line up with the remedy names. It was available for the profession in 1892.
Afterwards Dr H. C. Allen worked on Gurensey’s cards and added more remedies, which was known as
Allen’s-Boienninghausen’s cards.
Ref: Reperire, by Dr Vidyadhar R. Khanaj, page 654.
regional repertory
Particular / Regional clinical repertories These are those repertories which denote a particular part or a
particular clinical condition. For examples, Repertory of neuralgia.
Regional repertories these are those repertories, which pertain to different regions or parts of the body. These
repertories are useful in cases where there is special pathology or symptoms pertaining to any organ or part
of the body. In the years between 1890 and 1910 several regional repertories were published.

General repertory
It is based on the concept of generalization. In this type of repertory, the concept of totality is based on
analogy and concomitants. Particulars are augmented / upgraded to generals by above concepts. no further
differentiation of rubric is made.
Examples: Boienninghausen’s Therapeutic Pocket Book.
Ref: A Textbook of Homoeopathic Repertory, by Prof. niranjan Mohanty, page 40.
Generalization is an act or a process of arriving at generals out of particulars. For example, at different levels,
symptoms can be general. As:
Location:
When a particular symptoms is found at two or more locations it becomes general.
Location / Sensation and Pathology:
When a particular sensation / pathology is found at two or more places it becomes general. For example,
burning pain on vertex, burning pain on palm and sole and burning in abdomen. Then burning is considered
as a general symptom.
Modalities:
When a particular modality is found at two or more places it becomes a general one that is, sitiching pain in
the chest aggravated by motion and ameliorated by rest. Pain in joints aggravated by motion and better by
rest. Hence, aggravation on motion and amelioration on rest are generals.
Local pathology becomes a physical general / miasmatic background / interpretation :
(a) A solitary mole or wart – sycotic miasm.
(b) A localised patch or eczema – psoric miasm.
Constitution/ diathesis: for example
(a) Recurrent epistaxis – haemorrhagic diathesis.
(b) Recurrent colds – Hydrogenoid constitution.
